summary: This informational memo is an introductory guide to common TCP/IP and Internet tools and utilities. It also covers discussion lists, ways to obtain Internet documents, and resources for finding your way around the Internet.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a 1997 introduction to tools and services for finding hosts, moving files, exploring information, and locating Internet documents. The examples and services describe that period.

subtitle: A 1997 guide to common TCP/IP tools, Internet services, and RFC documents.

tldr.problem: New Internet users had many tools and services but needed a basic guide to their purposes and use.
tldr.mechanism: The memo demonstrates host lookup, connectivity checks, remote login, file transfer, information services, the Web, mailing lists, newsgroups, and ways to obtain Internet documents.
tldr.outcome: It is a snapshot of tools and services described in 1997. It is FYI 30, obsoletes RFC 1739, and states that security issues are not discussed.

today: RFC 2151 is an Informational memo, also FYI 30, published in June 1997. It obsoletes RFC 1739, and the tools and sites it describes reflect the period when it was written.

sections.title: How to Use the Primer
sections.content:
The memo is an introductory guide to commonly available TCP/IP and Internet tools. It is intended for self-study, a course laboratory manual, or the basis of a local user's guide, and points to other sources for more detail.

Its sample sessions come from several operating systems and command-line tools. The RFC warns that not every host has every tool and that interfaces vary between software packages.
sections.plainLanguage: The guide explains tools through descriptions and sample sessions. A particular computer may use different commands or may not include every tool shown.

sections.title: Finding and Testing Internet Hosts
sections.content:
NSLOOKUP queries the Domain Name System for records such as host addresses and mail exchangers. Ping uses ICMP Echo messages to check whether a host responds and to measure round-trip delay; its default request contains 56 data bytes.

Traceroute shows successive routers along a path. The classic method sends UDP datagrams with increasing Time-To-Live values; routers return ICMP Time Exceeded messages, and the destination's response ends the trace. The defaults described include a maximum of 30 hops, three probes per hop, a five-second wait, and port 33434.
sections.plainLanguage: NSLOOKUP asks DNS for information about a name or address. Ping checks for a response, while traceroute shows which routers respond along a path.

sections.title: Remote Login and File Transfer
sections.content:
TELNET provides a virtual terminal for logging in to a remote host. The memo also describes connecting to a service by giving its port number; for example, it identifies port 79 for Finger.

FTP transfers files between hosts. Anonymous FTP allows access to some archives without a pre-established account. The guide emphasizes selecting image or binary transfer mode for executable files and describes commands for listing directories, changing directories, and transferring files.
sections.plainLanguage: TELNET gives a user a remote terminal session. FTP moves files between computers and has a transfer mode for binary data.

sections.title: Directories, Information Services and the Web
sections.content:
WHOIS and NICNAME search registration databases for contacts and network information. KNOWBOT queries several user databases. Archie indexes files at anonymous FTP sites; Gopher organizes information in menus; VERONICA searches Gopher menu titles; JUGHEAD searches a Gopher server's menu database; and WAIS provides one interface to multiple information databases.

The Web uses browsers, URLs, and HTTP to connect documents and other resources. The memo also describes discussion lists, LISTSERV, Majordomo, and Usenet newsgroups, including the practice of sending administrative requests to a list server rather than to the discussion list.
sections.plainLanguage: The guide describes several directory and information-search tools from the 1990s. It also explains how Web pages, mailing lists, and newsgroups let users find and exchange information.

sections.title: RFCs and Other Internet Documents
sections.content:
The memo explains that RFCs cover protocols, standards, research, and general information, and that an RFC number is never reused. It distinguishes the STD series for standards, the FYI series for information aimed at a broad range of users, and the Best Current Practices series.

It describes obtaining documents through e-mail services, anonymous FTP, and Web sites. The final security section says that security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: RFCs are documents about Internet protocols and other topics. This guide also explains the STD, FYI, and BCP series and gives ways to retrieve documents.
